proposals.relationship: Lears identifies Gramsci’s account of cultural hegemony as a framework for rethinking power, consent and cultural meaning in American history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1985explicitly adopts a framework and vocabulary while declining an uncritical embrace of the revolutionary program. Hoare/Nowell Smith’s1971Prison Notebooks translation and Lawner’s1973Letters are specified witnesses, not the complete Italian corpus. Own2010recollection retains Genovese and Davis as interpreters in his graduate intellectual environment.
primary_locators: Printed567–571, especially568opening;568n3and570n7; own2010paragraph beginning As hopes for a New Left faded.

proposals.relationship: Lears questions Gramsci’s revolutionary teleology, rationalist psychology and rigid distinctions while retaining hegemony as a flexible historical method.
proposals.evidence_note: Own critique singles out organic/traditional intellectuals, assumptions about workers’ authentic interests and a force/consent polarity. He concludes by affirming Gramsci’s openness to contradictory experience. This is not rejection of the entire method. Originals beyond the cited translated selections unread.
primary_locators: Printed572intellectuals distinction;578–579teleology;586force/consent;593conclusion.

proposals.relationship: Lears invokes Thompson’s unintended-consequences formulation and his account of law’s relative autonomy when explaining cultural meaning and power.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Cohen answer expressly paraphrases Thompson, without establishing the original aphorism’s exact wording or source. Own1985p590uses Whigs and Hunters1975pp258–269 among plural models for ideology’s promise. Specific resources, not a claim to adopt all Thompson.
primary_locators: CohenIIanswer beginning One of the aphorisms;1985printed590first paragraph/n54.

proposals.relationship: Lears uses Williams’s account of feeling and cultural relations when developing a less mechanical conception of hegemony.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1985invokes structure of feeling and identifies a parallel base/superstructure argument;1973article and The Long Revolution1961pp48–71 are distinct cited works. This is Raymond, not Eric Williams. Complete originals unread.

proposals.relationship: Lears uses Genovese’s account of paternalism, accommodation and resistance to develop a historical analysis of hegemony.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1985draws on Roll, Jordan, Roll1974pp585–665 and separately In Red and Black1970p369. He explicitly says his summary simplifies a complex argument; slaves’ dignity and resistance remain alongside accommodation. Whole books unread.

proposals.relationship: Lears uses Davis’s analysis of abolitionism’s unintended consequences to extend hegemony beyond deliberate social control.

His2010mentor recollection is supplementary.

proposals.relationship: Lears questions antisubjectivist readings of Foucault and their capacity to explain agency and a shared political good.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1985recognizes salutary effects of socially constituted subjectivity before objecting to mechanistic agency-denial. Own2010distinguishes Foucault’s useful surveillance analysis from an individualist academic reception; it is not a claim that every recipient interpretation is Foucault’s own doctrine. Cited original books unread.
primary_locators: Printed592–593withn60;2010paragraphs The regnant modes of theory and But another side of Foucault.

proposals.relationship: Lears questions the historical usefulness of Habermas’s ideal speech situation as a possible alternative to hegemonic discourse.

Cites What Is Universal Pragmatics? in Communication and the Evolution of Society, Thomas McCarthy translation1979p63. This is a task-specific limitation, not rejection of all Habermas; original unread.

proposals.evidence_note: Own qualified note concerns Politics, Language, and Time1971,3–41; it accompanies proposals to study broader cultural texts and symbolic practices. No blanket rejection of intellectual history or a claim to have read Pocock’s entire book.
